It is characterized by involuntary rigidity and painful spasm of the axial muscles, resembling a chronic form of tetanus. 1–10 Patients are likened to ‘‘tin soldiers,’’ 2 with the following criteria: (1) initial stiffness and rigidity in the axial muscles; (2) slow progression of stiffness to include proximal limb muscles, making volitional movements and ambulation difficult; (3) a fixed deformity of the spine, as in lordosis, and with some patients a restriction of hip movement; (4) the presence of superimposed episodic spasms precipitated by sudden movements, jarring noise, and emotional upset; (5) normal findings on motor and sensory nerve examinations; (6) normal intellect; and (7) electromyographic findings typical of continuous motor activity that can be abolished by intravenous or orally administered diazepam.
